title: Turnovers: interceptions, fumbles and the "turnover-worthy play" (and why it matters for tonight's Under)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run. It still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, "Eagles at Bears, Week 3", no snaps logged) and no review files. The backup source (football-film-room, branch "data") couldn't be read: "GitHub access to this repository is not enabled for this session" (HTTP 403). So there's no new miss of yours to fix. It's a new concept tied to tonight's CMU-Buffalo game and Monday's Zay Flowers fumble. It builds on Lesson 28 (the strip-sack) and Lesson 46 (field position).

The big idea: a turnover is when the offense loses the ball to the defense.There are two kinds. An interception: a defender catches a pass. A fumble lost: the ball comes loose and the defense recovers it.Turnovers swing games and totals more than almost any other play. They hand the other team a short field, or even a touchdown.

QB = quarterback, WR = wide receiver, RB = running back, LB = linebacker. Red circles are defenders.

  1. A · Late over the middle. The QB waits too long, and a linebacker or safety drops into the throwing lane.This is the most common interception. The defender is already facing the QB.
  2. B · Into double coverage. Two defenders near one receiver. Even a good throw can be tipped.Ball State's Keldric Luster threw 1 INT Tuesday; Ohio's Nick Poulos threw 1 too.
  3. C · Ball loose in traffic. A runner carries the ball away from his body, and a second tackler punches at it.Monday: Zay Flowers lost a fumble late, and the Chargers held on 23-20.
  4. D · The blind-side swipe. A rusher the QB can't see hits the throwing arm. That's the strip-sack (Lesson 28).

The "turnover-worthy play": PFF tags any throw or carry that should have been a turnover, whether the defense caught it or not.Dropped interceptions count. That makes it a better guide to the future than a QB's actual interceptions, which include luck.A QB with lots of turnover-worthy plays but few interceptions has been lucky. Expect more turnovers ahead.

Tonight's example: Central Michigan QB Jadyn Glasser has the highest turnover-worthy play rate in FBS: 8.2% of his plays (Covers, from PFF).Buffalo QB Jason Wright has 16 turnover-worthy plays this season.That's the main risk for the board's CMU-Buffalo Under. One interception near midfield gives the other team a short field and maybe 7 easy points (Lesson 46).

Why it still can be an Under: both teams run first. CMU runs 41.3 times a game. Fewer passes means fewer chances to throw a pick.

For your Film Room drill: when you log a snap that ends in a turnover, note which kind: A, B, C or D.Then look at the next snap. A short field (inside the 40) makes a run call more likely: the offense is already close to field-goal range.On 3rd-and-long with a turnover-prone QB, many coaches call a safe run or a screen instead of a risky throw. Lean run.

Connecting the dots: Lesson 28 showed the strip-sack. Lesson 46 showed how a short field turns into points. Lesson 51 showed the pick-six. A turnover-worthy play is the warning sign before all three.

Video: search YouTube for "turnover worthy play explained PFF" and "Zay Flowers fumble Chargers Ravens."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 6: Situations)

quiz.q: What's the difference between an interception and a lost fumble?
o: An interception is a caught pass by the defense; a lost fumble is a loose ball the defense recovers
A fumble only happens on kicks
An interception only counts in the end zone
quiz.w: Both are turnovers. An interception is a defender catching a pass. A fumble lost is a loose ball the defense picks up.

quiz.q: Why is a "turnover-worthy play" rate a better guide than a QB's interception count?
o: It counts risky plays even when the defense dropped the ball, so it takes luck out
It's the same as the interception count
quiz.w: Dropped interceptions still count as turnover-worthy plays. That shows how risky the QB really is, not how lucky he's been.

quiz.q: CMU's QB has the highest turnover-worthy play rate in FBS. What does that do to the board's CMU-Buffalo Under?
o: It's the main risk: a turnover can give Buffalo a short field and quick points
It means CMU will pass more
quiz.w: A turnover near midfield turns into easy points (Lesson 46). That's why it's a lean, not a pick.

quiz.q: In your drill, the defense just intercepted at the offense's 35. The new offense has 1st-and-10 there. What's the better lean?
o: Run: they're already near field-goal range and don't need to take risks
quiz.w: A short field lets the offense play it safe. Runs and short throws are common right after a turnover in good field position.
